geoWhatText: PhotoEngraving.online is a free browser-based image to laser engraving converter. It converts photos into laser-ready black-and-white PNG or 1-bit BMP files with DPI metadata for LightBurn, XCS, LaserGRBL, EZCAD and similar laser software.
geoWhoTitle: Who is this laser engraving converter for?
geoWhoText: This tool is made for makers, laser engraving users and small workshops that need to prepare photos for engraving on wood, plywood, slate, anodized aluminum, stainless steel, leather and other materials before importing the file into laser software.
geoFormatsTitle: PNG or BMP for LightBurn, XCS, LaserGRBL and EZCAD
geoFormatsText: Export PNG for most workflows, or 1-bit BMP when you need a strict black-and-white bitmap. Both exports include DPI metadata so the physical size is easier to keep consistent in laser software.
geoAboutText: PhotoEngraving.online was created for users who need a simple way to prepare photos for laser engraving without installing desktop software. The editor runs locally in the browser, supports real size in millimeters, custom DPI, dithering, material preview and exports ready for common laser engraving programs. Last updated: October 2026.
faq1Question: Is this photo to laser engraving converter free?
faq1Answer: Yes. The tool is free to use in your browser. You can convert a photo to a laser engraving PNG and download the result without installing software.
faq2Question: Which laser software can use the exported PNG?
faq2Answer: The PNG output is suitable for LightBurn, XCS, LaserGRBL, EZCAD and other laser engraving software that imports raster images.
faq3Question: Does the PNG include DPI information?
faq3Answer: Yes. The exported PNG includes DPI metadata, which helps laser software keep the correct physical engraving size.
faq4Question: Can I use my own DPI value?
faq4Answer: Yes. You can choose a preset DPI or enter a custom DPI value for your laser, material and preferred line spacing.
faq5Answer: Negative creates an inverted output by swapping black and white in the final laser-ready image.
faq6Question: Are my photos uploaded to a server?
faq6Answer: No. Photos are processed locally in your browser and are not uploaded to our server.
faq7Answer: You can preview wood, slate, dark anodized or coated surfaces, stainless steel and leather. The preview is approximate and should always be verified with a test engraving.
faq8Question: Should I export PNG or BMP for laser engraving?
faq8Answer: PNG is recommended for most laser software. Use 1-bit BMP when your workflow needs a strict black-and-white bitmap.
faq9Question: What DPI should I use for photo engraving?
faq9Answer: Start with 254 DPI for wood, plywood, MDF, slate and stone, 300 DPI for general use, and 508 DPI for finer materials such as acrylic, laminates and coated metals.
guideAriaLabel: Open laser photo engraving user guide
hintLine: Start right away with the demo photo or upload your own
zoomHelp: Move the mouse over the image to inspect details in the magnifier. On touch devices, hold and drag over the image. For the best experience and more comfortable editing, we recommend using this tool on a desktop computer.
dropZoneMain: Drag & drop or click to choose
cropModalText: Drag to draw a crop area. Drag inside the area to move it, or drag a corner to resize it.
presetHelp: Default is Normal Photo. Choose Negative for an inverted output, or fine-tune everything with the sliders below.
ditherHelp: Floyd-Steinberg is the balanced choice. Atkinson is softer, Jarvis is smoother with more tones, and Ordered/Bayer creates a regular pattern (suitable for logos and graphics).
ditherComparisonTitle: Compare dithering methods on your photo
ditherComparisonIntro: All four previews use the same crop, tonal adjustments and Photo Type. Use the button below a preview to apply that method to the main laser-ready output.
ditherFloydDescription: Balanced contrast and detail. A reliable first choice for most photographs and materials.
ditherAtkinsonDescription: A lighter, softer pattern that can keep skin tones and heat-sensitive materials cleaner.
ditherJarvisDescription: Smooth tonal transitions with a denser pattern. Useful when the material can hold fine dots.
ditherOrderedDescription: A regular, visible dot pattern. Best for graphic looks, raster logos and predictable repetition.
recommendPortraitText: Start with Floyd-Steinberg. Try Atkinson when skin or highlights look too dark. Use Normal Photo on light materials and Negative on dark surfaces.
recommendLogoText: Start with Ordered / Bayer for a regular raster pattern. For clean outlines and solid shapes, a vector logo in your laser software is usually better than dithering.
recommendWoodText: Start with 254 DPI and Floyd-Steinberg. Try Atkinson if dots spread or shadows burn together. Keep dark areas open and test on the same wood.
recommendSlateText: Start with Negative, 254–300 DPI and Floyd-Steinberg. Try Jarvis for smoother tones if the slate keeps fine light marks.
recommendMetalText: For dark anodized or coated metal, start with Negative and Floyd-Steinberg or Jarvis. Use 300–508 DPI only when the laser spot and coating can reproduce it. Bare stainless steel, marking spray and fiber marking require separate tests.
materialPowerHelp: Adjusts only the Material Preview. On wood and leather, more power can look darker and spread more. On dark coated surfaces, too much power can make the light mark turn dull gray and reduce contrast. The exported PNG/BMP stays unchanged.
outputWidthMmHelp: Enter the real engraving width in millimeters.
dpiHelp: Changing DPI keeps the same physical size and recalculates the pixel count.
customDpiHelp: Enter your own DPI value between 1 and 2400.
outputSliderHelp: Advanced control. Changing pixels recalculates the width in mm for the selected DPI.
exportHelp: PNG is recommended for LightBurn, XCS, LaserGRBL and other laser software. PNG and 1-bit BMP include DPI metadata for the correct physical size in laser software.

materialPreviewDisclaimer: This is an approximate visual simulation only. Real results depend on laser type, lens, focus, speed, power and the exact material surface. The downloaded PNG/BMP remains the clean black-and-white laser-ready output.
materialTipNone: Select a material to see an approximate preview of how the engraved image may look on the surface.
materialTipWood: Birch plywood and light wood usually engrave darker than the surface. Expect some dot gain, especially on plywood and softer wood.
materialTipSlate: Slate and dark stone usually engrave lighter than the surface. Negative mode is often the right starting point.
materialTipBlackAnodized: Dark anodized, coated or painted surfaces often engrave lighter at first. Too much power can make the mark darker gray and lower the contrast, so test a small crop before engraving the final piece.
materialTipStainless: Stainless steel preview is only approximate. Higher preview power increases mark darkness, but it does not simulate the burnt edge spread used for wood. Real results depend strongly on fiber/diode laser type, marking spray, focus, speed and power.
materialTipLeather: Leather usually engraves darker and can spread slightly. Lower detail and test pieces are recommended.
helpIntroText: Photo Engraving Online prepares a normal photo for laser engraving by controlling crop, tones, dithering, output size and DPI. The result is a black-and-white PNG or BMP you can import into LightBurn, XCS, LaserGRBL, EZCAD and similar laser software.
helpStep1Text: Click Upload photo and choose a JPG, PNG, BMP or WebP file. For best results, start with a sharp photo, clear lighting and visible detail in the subject.
helpStep2Text: Start with Normal Photo, Negative, Dark Photo or Light Photo. Then choose the dithering pattern: Floyd-Steinberg is a balanced default, Atkinson is softer, Jarvis keeps smoother tones, and Ordered/Bayer is useful for graphic, regular-dot looks.
helpStep3Title: Tune the image and Material Preview
helpStep3Text: Adjust brightness, contrast, gamma and sharpness while comparing the original with the output. Then use Material Preview to get a rough idea of how the file may behave on wood, slate, dark surfaces, stainless steel or leather.
helpStep4Text: Enter the real engraving width in millimeters, choose 254, 300, 508 or Custom DPI, and watch the pixel count update. If the preview looks right, download PNG or 1-bit BMP with DPI metadata and import it into your laser software.
helpDpi254Material: Soft wood, soft plywood, MDF, slate, stone
helpDpi508Material: Acrylic, laminates, coated metals, anodized aluminum, stainless steel
helpOutputSizeTitle: How to choose the correct output size?
helpOutputSizeText1: The output size in mm should exactly match the real physical size of the engraving area on your material.
helpOutputSizeText2: Example: If you want to engrave a portrait on a wooden plate with a width of 80 mm, set the width to 80 mm and choose 254 DPI. The tool will create an image about 800 px wide. Changing DPI keeps the same physical size but recalculates the pixel count, and the advanced pixel-width control can fine-tune the final raster when your laser software needs an exact pixel size.
helpOutputSizeFormula: ℹ️ Formula: width in px = (width in mm ÷ 25.4) × DPI
helpTip1Text: Use sharp, evenly lit photos with visible detail in the face, object or texture. Crop away empty background before dithering so the laser-ready pixels focus on the important area.
helpTip2Text: Switch between Original + Output, Output and Material Preview. The simulation is only a guide, but the power slider can warn you when stronger settings may darken, spread or flatten the real mark.
helpTip3Text: Always test on an offcut of the same material. Real results still depend on laser type, focus, lens, speed, power, coating and the exact surface.
helpTip4Text: Import the PNG or BMP as Passthrough or Threshold. The dithering is already included in the file, so additional image processing may make it worse. Use the embedded DPI metadata or manually set the same physical width if your software ignores metadata.
